title: Solve Multiple Equations With List Regression
description: Pair equation sides in equal-length lists to solve systems, combine function conditions, apply restrictions, and find fixed ratios using a legal free base.

blocks.html:
Two equations, one calculator row

You already know that ~ asks Desmos to find unknown values. Here it is working on two equations together:

\[a+b=11\qquad a-b=3\]

Read the assigned values below the bracketed expression. Then change the last number on the right from \(3\) to \(5\). Watch both values update. Use Reset to restore the original problem.

Before starting: Be comfortable reading regression values and using square brackets for lists. The later examples also use function notation and percents.

content.prompt: For the original system \(a+b=11\) and \(a-b=3\), which pair satisfies both equations?
content.explanation: The readout gives \(a=7\) and \(b=4\): their sum is 11 and their difference is 3. The pair must satisfy both conditions.
content.hint: Check the sum and the difference of the same pair.

blocks.html:
Pair the sides

The move: Left sides in one list, right sides in the other, in matching order.

Why it pays: You can enter several equations without isolating a variable first.

One caution: Desmos fits what you type. A misplaced entry changes which equations it solves.

A system is a group of equations that must be true together. A list puts entries inside square brackets, separated by commas. For list regression, each matching position represents one equation:

\[[a+b,\ a-b]\sim[11,\ 3]\]

  • First with first: \(a+b=11\).
  • Second with second: \(a-b=3\).

Pair the sides: Each equation contributes one entry to each list.

content.explanation: The first entries encode \(2m+n=17\); the second encode \(m-n=4\). Reversing just the right list would attach each expression to the wrong number.
content.hint: Read the first entries as one equation, then the second entries as another.

blocks.html:
Use the same four steps

  1. Collect. Write the equations and note the problem’s restrictions.
  2. Pair. Put left sides and matching right sides in equal-length lists.
  3. Regress. Type one ~ between the lists. Leave unknowns free; do not create sliders for them.
  4. Check and answer. Read the fitted values, check the original conditions, and calculate the requested quantity.

Lowercase \(x\) and \(y\) have graphing jobs. Use \(X\) and \(Y\) for those unknowns, then translate back when answering. Other unknowns can keep their names.

One shared fit: Separate regression rows do not make the equations one simultaneous system. Put the related conditions together.

content.prompt: Which entry uses list regression for \(x+y=12\) and \(x-2y=3\)?
content.explanation: Use uppercase \(X,Y\), keep the matching sides together, and connect the lists with \(\sim\). Report the result using the original \(x,y\).
content.hint: Check the letter case, the tilde, and which entries are paired.

blocks.html:
Read the values, then check the fit

The REGRESSION PARAMETERS section gives the values Desmos fitted. RMSE measures the mismatch between paired entries. For these exact-equation problems, look for zero or a very small value, then substitute into the original conditions.

A small error is a useful check, not proof that the answer is unique. A visibly nonzero error means you should inspect the entries or try another method.

The fitted values stay assigned. If the question asks for \(2a+b\), type 2a+b on another row to calculate it.

Answer the requested quantity: RMSE is an error measure, not the answer.

content.title: Build the paired lists
content.instructions_html:
Enter \(2u+v=19\) and \(u-v=2\) as one list-regression row in this blank calculator. Keep each complete side intact.

Either equation may come first if you move its matching side with it. You may also reverse an equation’s two sides. Submit the row, then read both fitted values and inspect RMSE.

feedback.success_message_html: The conditions are paired correctly. Desmos fits \(u=7\) and \(v=5\).
feedback.retry_message_html: Use one row with two square-bracket lists and one tilde. Keep each complete side as written, and check which entries line up.
feedback.solution_html: Enter \([2u+v,u-v]\sim[19,2]\). Desmos assigns \(u=7\) and \(v=5\); the paired values match with zero or tiny RMSE.

content.prompt: The regression fitted \(u=7\) and \(v=5\). What is \(3u-v\)?
content.explanation: Typing \(3u-v\) gives \(16\). The SAT asked for the expression, not either fitted value.
content.hint: Use the two fitted values in the requested expression.
content.solution:
Keep the fitted values assigned, or enter them in this scratch calculator as \(u=7\) and \(v=5\).
Type \(3u-v\). The result is \(16\).

blocks.html:
Keep the function; pair its conditions

Suppose \(f(x)=a(x-2)^2+b\), with \(f(0)=17\) and \(a+b=8\).

Keep the function definition on its own row with an equals sign:

\[f(x)=a(x-2)^2+b\]

Then put the two conditions together:

\[[f(0),a+b]\sim[17,8]\]

The \(x\) inside the definition is the function’s input. It can stay lowercase because we are fitting \(a,b\), not solving for that input.

Definitions still have a job: Define a function before calling it. The list regression combines the conditions used to find its constants.

content.prompt: The function \(g\) is defined by \(g(x)=c(x-1)^2+d\). If \(g(3)=22\) and \(c+d=10\), what is \(c\)?
content.explanation: Define \(g\), then enter \([g(3),c+d]\sim[22,10]\). Desmos fits \(c=4,d=6\). Report \(4\).
content.hint: Give the function its definition, then collect the two conditions into matching lists.
content.solution:
Enter \(g(x)=c(x-1)^2+d\).
Enter \([g(3),c+d]\sim[22,10]\).
Desmos assigns \(c=4,d=6\). Read \(c\): the answer is \(4\).

blocks.html:
A fit is one solution

The system \(r+s=13\), \(rs=40\) has two pairs: \((8,5)\) and \((5,8)\). Enter the paired lists and note which one Desmos finds.

Either pair gives zero error. The readout does not list the entire solution set.

Choose the method for the question: If you need every solution or a solution count, use graphing or algebra to establish them. One regression result is not enough.

content.prompt: Regression returns \(r=8,s=5\) for \(r+s=13,\ rs=40\). Which conclusion follows?
content.explanation: The swapped pair \((5,8)\) also satisfies both equations. A successful fit establishes a working pair, not the number of pairs.
choices: The other pair has a larger RMSE.
The solution count is the displayed RMSE.
This pair works; another pair can also work.
content.hint: Compare what happens when the two values trade places.

blocks.html:
Carry the restriction into the search

Now suppose the same problem states \(r>s\). Add that condition in braces after the right list:

\[[r+s,rs]\sim[13,40]\{r>s\}\]

Desmos should fit \(r=8,s=5\). The restriction selects the pair allowed by the question.

Use the same idea for positivity or a stated interval, such as \(\{k>0\}\) or \(\{2

Use the given condition: Do not invent a restriction just to force a preferred answer.

content.prompt: The positive numbers \(m,n\) satisfy \(m+n=15\) and \(mn=54\). If \(m<n\), what is \(m\)?
content.explanation: Enter \([m+n,mn]\sim[15,54]\{m<n\}\). The fitted values are \(m=6,n=9\), consistent with the positive-number condition.
content.hint: Keep the two equation pairs and include the stated ordering in braces.
content.solution:
Enter \([m+n,mn]\sim[15,54]\{m<n\}\).
Read \(m=6,n=9\). Both are positive and the first is smaller.
The requested value is \(6\).

blocks.html:
Relative amounts let you choose a base

A sample’s weight \(A\) is \(240\%\) of weight \(B\), and \(A\) is \(0.8\%\) of weight \(C\). The question asks: \(C\) is what percent \(p\) of \(B\)?

Only ratios are fixed. Choose B=1 to represent one unit of the base weight. This is a convenient scale, not a claim that the sample weighs one gram.

Then pair all three statements:

\[[A,A,C]\sim[2.4B,0.008C,(p/100)B]\]

Percent means “divide by 100”: \(240\%=2.4\), \(0.8\%=0.008\), and \(p\%=p/100\). Decimal multipliers keep the entries compact.

Choose only a free amount: A stated weight must keep its given value.

content.prompt: In that relative-weight problem, why can you define \(B=1\)?
content.explanation: Changing the common weight scale preserves the percent comparisons. Choose B; the equations determine the corresponding A and C.
choices: The requested percent fixes B at one gram.
Scaling the weights together preserves their ratios.
Regression requires the letter B to equal one.
One equation lets you choose every weight separately.
content.hint: Ask whether multiplying all three weights by the same positive factor changes any comparison.

blocks.html:
Do not let zero erase the question

If all three weights are left free, \(A=B=C=0\) satisfies those entered equations for any \(p\). Zero RMSE would not identify the percent.

Defining B=1 removes that meaningless case. In a fresh calculator, enter it and then the three-pair regression from the previous example. Read \(A,C,p\).

Check the context: Sample weights are positive. A zero-weight fit cannot answer this comparison.

content.prompt: Weight \(A\) is \(240\%\) of weight \(B\) and \(0.8\%\) of weight \(C\). Weight \(C\) is \(p\%\) of weight \(B\). What is \(p\)?
content.explanation: With \(B=1\), the regression gives \(A=2.4,C=300,p=30000\). A multiplier of 300 is 30,000 percent, so report \(30000\).
content.hint: Fix the free base, then include the requested percent as the third paired condition.
content.solution:
Enter \(B=1\).
Enter \([A,A,C]\sim[2.4B,0.008C,(p/100)B]\).
Read the fitted parameter \(p=30000\). The value \(C=300\) is the multiplier, not the percent.

blocks.html:
Know when a chosen value changes the problem

Choosing \(B=1\) worked because the question fixed ratios and asked for a ratio. It did not fix an actual weight.

If the question instead gives \(B=75\) grams, enter that given value. If it asks for an actual weight and provides only ratios, choosing a base does not uncover a unique weight.

The target must stay fixed: Convenient values help only when the requested answer is unchanged across the allowed choices.

content.prompt: A problem states that sample B weighs 75 grams. What should replace the base definition from the previous example?
content.explanation: Keep the supplied measurement. Choosing a different base here would change the actual-weight problem.
content.hint: Distinguish a free reference scale from a measurement supplied in the question.

blocks.html:
Advanced: two conditions with powers

Suppose \(p>1\), \(t>1\), and

\[p^{3/4}=t^{5/2}\qquad t=p^{2n-1}.\]

Pair the sides just as before:

\[[p^{3/4},t]\sim[t^{5/2},p^{2n-1}]\{p>1\}\{t>1\}\]

The restrictions matter. At \(p=t=1\), both equations would hold regardless of \(n\). That case is forbidden by the problem.

Same brackets, harder expressions: Keep the whole fraction or expression inside its exponent.

content.prompt: Why would allowing \(p=t=1\) fail to determine \(n\) in the power equations?
content.explanation: Both sides become 1 regardless of \(n\). The problem excludes that case with \(p>1,t>1\).
choices: The first equation would have a negative side.
The second equation would force n to be 1.
The two lists would have different lengths.
content.hint: Evaluate a few different powers with base 1.

blocks.html:
A legal base can simplify this fit

For these particular equations, each allowed \(p>1\) leads to the same \(n\): the first relationship fixes the power connecting \(t\) to \(p\), and the second describes that same power.

You can therefore define p=2 and enter:

\[[p^{3/4},t]\sim[t^{5/2},p^{2n-1}]\{t>1\}\]

Try it in a fresh calculator. Then change the definition to p=3. Compare \(t\) and \(n\) in the two runs. This is a check on the setup; two numerical trials alone do not prove a general rule.

A useful combination: Fix a legal free base, then let list regression connect the remaining quantities.

content.prompt: For \(p^{3/4}=t^{5/2}\) and \(t=p^{2n-1}\), where \(p>1,t>1\), what value of \(n\) does the regression give?
content.explanation: The fit gives \(n=0.65=13/20\). Changing the legal base changes \(t\), while this value of \(n\) stays the same.
content.hint: Use a legal fixed p and enter both full power expressions in matching positions.
content.solution:
Enter \(p=2\).
Enter \([p^{3/4},t]\sim[t^{5/2},p^{2n-1}]\{t>1\}\).
Read \(n=0.65\). Enter \(13/20\) to confirm the same decimal.

blocks.html:
Reach for it when the conditions pin down the answer

List regression fits a short set of exact equations. Check equal list lengths, matching positions, and every stated condition. If an unknown already has a slider or another definition, remove that assignment so regression can fit it.

A nonzero fit error may signal a typo, inconsistent conditions, or a difficult numerical search. Recheck the original problem and use graphing or algebra if the fit remains unreliable.

For an identity that holds for every input, use several fixed inputs as taught in the equivalent-expressions lesson. For measured data and a best-fit model, use the data-regression lessons.

One fitted pair is enough only when it determines what the question asks.

content.prompt: The function \(h\) is defined by \(h(x)=a(x-3)^2+b\), where \(a\) and \(b\) are constants. If \(h(1)=26\) and \(a+b=11\), what is the value of \(a-b\)?
content.explanation: Define \(h(x)=a(x-3)^2+b\), then enter \([h(1),a+b]\sim[26,11]\). The fitted values are \(a=5,b=6\). Typing \(a-b\) gives \(-1\).

content.prompt: Two equations, two unknowns. Recall “pair the sides”: how do you build the regression and finish?
content.explanation: Matching positions preserve the equations. The tilde fits their unknowns together; the conditions and requested quantity decide what you report.
choices: Pair left sides with right sides in matching order; use = between the lists; check conditions and evaluate the requested quantity.
Pair left sides with right sides in separate orders; use ~ between the lists; check conditions and evaluate the requested quantity.
Pair left sides with right sides in matching order; use ~ between the lists; report RMSE as the requested quantity.
Pair left sides with right sides in matching order; use ~ between the lists; check conditions and evaluate the requested quantity.

blocks.html:
Your turn to choose the setup

The last problem gives relative amounts and asks for a percent. Build a legal base and translate the conditions yourself. Use a fresh scratch calculator so earlier assignments do not interfere.

content.prompt: The mass of sample R is 360% of the mass of sample S and 0.9% of the mass of sample T. If the mass of sample T is \(q\%\) of the mass of sample S, what is the value of \(q\)?
content.explanation: Define \(S=1\), then enter \([R,R,T]\sim[3.6S,0.009T,(q/100)S]\). Desmos fits \(R=3.6,T=400,q=40000\). The requested percent is \(40000\), not the multiplier \(400\).

content.html:
Pair the sides

When several exact conditions determine the answer, put them to work in one list regression.
